item.title: Preface
item.description: There are two influential textbooks on computer science: one was written 30 years ago, and the other was written 50 years ago. Computers were very different back then. A lot of this book discusses hardware. I am a software developer with no formal training in hardware, so on some occasions I might be misleading or wrong. All I am trying to do is to help you build a useful mental model.

item.title: Summary
item.description: Now we have enough information to summarize what we’ve learned. Loop unrolling. Here is a checklist (from easiest to hardest): Turn on optimization (-march=native, -O3, -ffast-math, -funroll-loops) Determine whether the algorithm is memory-bound or compute-bound. Blocking: try to split data in parts that fit cache Memory access patterns: try to linearize every reads Prefetching: if access pattern is not well predictable, or port is free, add a prefetching step Branching: remove branching Loop Unrolling: #pragma GCC unroll n Data Dependencies: consult and instruction table or llvm-mca SIMD: simplify a loop Arithmetic: use smallest type available and turn on -ffast-math Temporal locality Allocations Profile stuff

item.title: Probability Theory Refresher
item.description: Throughout this book, we will extensively use probability theory both to design faster algorithms and assess them. This section is a brief refresher on statistics for computer science. It is designed to take you all the way from definitions of random variables to statistical significance and modelling without leaving any proofs behind in about 40 minutes or so. #BasicsA random variable is any variable whose value depends on an outcome of a random event.
